doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

chapter: Rock and roll, Elvis and Sinatra
title: Colonel Parker and Sinatra's reinvention
summary: Brief comment on Parker, then Sinatra as first teenage star, his comeback, and Italian-American women in Buffalo going to his concerts.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: What do you think about Colonel Tom Parker?
Oh well, he’s just a character. He was making money.

You know, when he worked with Eddie Arnold, he only worked with Eddie Arnold. When he worked with Hank Snow, he only worked with Hank Snow. And then Elvis was one of the openers and I guess he saw him at one of those little airport things and — the guys didn’t get pissed off that the girls were in love with him. They said wow, I want to dress like that. I want to do something like that guy. He’s different than us. And we think we’re rocks and everything, but look at the style this guy’s got. And that’s unusual. You know, I just did a thing on Sinatra. When he was the first teenage star and he was singing all these beautiful ballads, you know, at the Paramount, and the girls are screaming and yelling, “Violets for Your Furs” right? They were still screaming when he’d do something like that. Those young guys hated that. They hated it. A skinny kid with a bow tie you know. But he reinvented himself and, you know, the Ava thing went, he lost his voice, he made the comeback after “Mama Won’t Bark” with Mitch Miller. And then all of a sudden he started doing these albums with ties down, you know, before “Only the Lonely.” You know, a drink in his hand. And what was it that Scott Fitzgerald said, “No second lives in America.” He reinvented himself. All of a sudden now here is a guy that these guys, when they were younger, suddenly thought were really cool now. How many

times has that happened? You know? He was something. My people loved him. Oh my God. When he played Buffalo, you could hear the jewelry being put on by his Italian women, from blocks away. “I don’t care,” the wives would tell their husbands, “I don’t care, you’re getting me tickets to the Memorial Auditorium. I don’t care what it costs, you take out a loan. You’re out there with the boys drinking, you’re doing this, we’re going to see Frank or you ain’t getting sex for the next month.”
